entities.name: Principia Mathematica (Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica)
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Published on 5 July 1687 by Isaac Newton (1642–1727), the Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica is widely considered the most influential scientific work ever published. In three books, Newton sets forth: his three laws of motion (inertia, F=ma, action-reaction); the law of universal gravitation (every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them); and the application of these principles to explain Kepler's laws of planetary motion, the tides, the precession of the equinoxes, the orbits of comets, and the shape of the Earth.

For the first time in human history, a single mathematical framework unified terrestrial and celestial mechanics — the same force that causes an apple to fall governs the motion of the Moon and planets. The Principia inaugurated the Newtonian paradigm that dominated physics for over 200 years (until Einstein's relativity) and demonstrated the power of mathematical reasoning to reveal the deep structure of nature.

Edmond Halley financed its publication and used Newton's methods to predict the return of Halley's Comet.
